title: "Logistic regression"

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 110,
                      message = FALSE)
library(ggplot2)
library(RColorBrewer)
library(MASS)
pal <- brewer.pal(8, "Paired")
theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = 13))
```

*Session 14 of the [course](index.html) · [Slides for this session (PDF)](slides/14-generalised-linear-models.pdf)*

**Learning goals.** After this lesson you can

- explain why a linear model is unsuitable for a binary outcome;
- explain the idea of maximum likelihood estimation;
- fit a logistic regression and interpret its coefficients as odds ratios;
- turn predicted probabilities into classifications and evaluate them on new data.

## The data

The `Pima.tr` and `Pima.te` data sets in the `MASS` package come from a study of
women of Pima Indian heritage aged 21 or older. The outcome `type` records
whether a woman has diabetes. We use `Pima.tr` (200 women) to fit models and
`Pima.te` (332 women) to test them.

```{r data}
train <- Pima.tr
test  <- Pima.te
train$diabetes <- as.integer(train$type == "Yes")
test$diabetes  <- as.integer(test$type == "Yes")
head(train)
mean(train$diabetes)
```

Let us start with one predictor: plasma glucose concentration (`glu`) from an
oral glucose tolerance test. Because the outcome is 0 or 1, many points overlap.
Adding a little random noise (*jittering*) makes them visible:

```{r plot-data}
p <- ggplot(train, aes(glu, diabetes)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0, height = 0.05, alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "Plasma glucose", y = "Diabetes (1 = yes)")
p
```

## Why not a straight line?

```{r linear-fit}
p + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = pal[6])
```

A straight line predicts "probabilities" below 0 and above 1 at the extremes,
and assumes that each extra unit of glucose changes the probability by the same
amount everywhere. Logistic regression instead models the **log-odds**:

$$\log\frac{p}{1-p} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x, \qquad
p = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x)}}.$$

The S-shaped curve always stays between 0 and 1.

## How are the coefficients estimated? Maximum likelihood

Least squares is no longer appropriate, so logistic regression uses **maximum
likelihood**: choose the parameter values under which the observed data are
most likely. For independent observations $z_1, \dots, z_n$ the likelihood is

$$L(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} f(z_i \mid \theta), \qquad
\log L(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log f(z_i \mid \theta).$$

**Comparing two explanations.** We observe the values 0 and 3 and propose that
they come either from $N(1, 2^2)$ or from $N(2, 1^2)$. Which explanation makes
the data more likely?

```{r ml-compare}
x <- c(0, 3)
c("N(1, 2)" = sum(dnorm(x, mean = 1, sd = 2, log = TRUE)),
  "N(2, 1)" = sum(dnorm(x, mean = 2, sd = 1, log = TRUE)))
```

The log-likelihood is higher for $N(1, 2^2)$: the wider distribution accounts
better for two observations that lie far apart.

**Searching over all values.** Suppose 6 of 10 patients respond to a treatment.
The likelihood of a response probability $p$ is $p^6(1-p)^4$:

```{r ml-curve, fig.height = 3.8}
p_grid <- seq(0.01, 0.99, 0.01)
loglik <- 6 * log(p_grid) + 4 * log(1 - p_grid)
plot(p_grid, loglik, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = pal[2],
     xlab = "p", ylab = "log-likelihood")
abline(v = p_grid[which.max(loglik)], lty = 2)
p_grid[which.max(loglik)]
```

The maximum is at $p = 0.6$, the observed proportion. `glm()` does the same for
the coefficients of a logistic regression, searching numerically for the values
that maximise the likelihood of the observed outcomes.

## Fitting the model

```{r glm}
fit <- glm(diabetes ~ glu, data = train, family = binomial)
summary(fit)
```

```{r glm-plot}
p + geom_smooth(method = "glm", method.args = list(family = binomial),
                colour = pal[2])
```

### Interpreting the coefficients

The slope is a change in log-odds, which is hard to interpret directly.
Exponentiating it gives an **odds ratio**:

```{r odds-ratio}
exp(coef(fit))
exp(confint(fit))
```

Each additional unit of glucose multiplies the odds of diabetes by about
`r round(exp(coef(fit)[2]), 3)`. For a 10-unit difference the odds are
multiplied by $`r round(exp(coef(fit)[2]), 3)`^{10} \approx `r round(exp(10 * coef(fit)[2]), 2)`$.

At which glucose level is the predicted probability exactly 0.5? Then the
log-odds are zero, so $x = -\beta_0/\beta_1$:

```{r p-half}
-coef(fit)[1] / coef(fit)[2]
```

## Several predictors

```{r glm-multi}
fit2 <- glm(diabetes ~ glu + bmi + age + ped, data = train, family = binomial)
round(cbind(odds_ratio = exp(coef(fit2)), exp(confint(fit2))), 3)
```

Each odds ratio now compares women who differ in one predictor while the others
are held constant. `ped` is a diabetes pedigree function, a score summarising
family history of diabetes.

## From probabilities to classifications

`predict(..., type = "response")` returns predicted probabilities. A common
(but not obligatory) rule classifies a woman as "diabetes" when the probability
exceeds 0.5. A fair test of a model uses data that were **not** used to fit it:

```{r predict}
test$prob <- predict(fit2, newdata = test, type = "response")
test$pred <- as.integer(test$prob > 0.5)
table(predicted = test$pred, observed = test$diabetes)
mean(test$pred == test$diabetes)   # accuracy
```

```{r sens-spec}
c(sensitivity = mean(test$pred[test$diabetes == 1] == 1),
  specificity = mean(test$pred[test$diabetes == 0] == 0))
```

Accuracy alone hides an important trade-off. **Sensitivity** is the proportion
of women with diabetes who are correctly identified; **specificity** is the
proportion without diabetes who are correctly identified. Lowering the
threshold raises sensitivity and lowers specificity. Which balance is
acceptable depends on the cost of missing a case compared with the cost of a
false alarm.

## Try it yourself

1. Change the classification threshold to 0.3. How do sensitivity and
   specificity change? When might a screening programme prefer this threshold?
2. Compute accuracy on the *training* data and compare it with the test data.
   Why is the training accuracy a too optimistic estimate?
3. Using the built-in `mtcars` data, model transmission type (`am`, 1 = manual)
   with `mpg` and `hp`. Interpret the odds ratio for `hp`.
